newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Who is who in Moldova's presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Who is who in Moldova's presidential election.

text.p: Following are brief portraits of the three main candidates in Moldova's first multi-party presidential election to be held on Sunday.
All of them rose to prominence in Soviet times and now occupy the three top posts in the tiny state landlocked between Ukraine and Romania.

MIRCEA SNEGUR, 56. President, elected on December 8, 1991. The tall, bulky and dark-haired Snegur has based his campaign on fostering an image of a kind man close to the people, who can no longer tolerate his nation's hardships or corrupt officials.

Centre-right Snegur, backed by his Party of Revival and Harmony and several nationalist parties, says he would dismiss the "corrupt and incompetent" government and parliament, both headed by his rivals, and amend the constitution to create a presidential republic, if he won.
Snegur favours closer ties with the West and Romania, and is cooler than his rivals over relations with Russia -- Moldova's prime provider of energy and fuel.
Snegur, an agronomist by education, was in charge of agriculture in Moldova's Communist Party before being elected, in 1989, head of the republican parliament.

ANDREI SANGHELI, 52. Prime Minister appointed by parliament in March 1994. Of medium-height, soft-spoken Sangheli has cultivated an image of a professional who prefers to act rather than to speak or be dragged into political intrigues.

Sangheli, backed by the Agrarian Democratic Party which has the biggest parliamentary faction, favours closer ties with Russia and deeper economic integration with the Commonwealth of Independent States.

Sangheli has achieved relative economic stabilisation and the country's reform programme is backed by the International Monetary Fund. He is a strong critic of the nationalists who want Moldova and Romania, which share a common language and culture, to unite.
Sangheli made his career in agriculture and in 1989 he became deputy prime minister. In 1990 he was appointed agriculture minister.

PETRU LUCINSCHI, 56. Parliament Chairman, elected in March 1994. Tall, bespectacled and charismatic, Lucinschi presents himself as a moderate, following the path of European social democracy. He is running as an independent but is backed by a number of leftist parties.
Lucinschi stands somewhere in between Snegur and Sangheli and favours equally close ties with East and West.
Good relations with Russia are one of the key issues in Lucinschi's programme. He calls Romanians "brothers", but rejects any prospects of a merger and talks mostly about economic relations.
Lucinschi, a historian, ruled Moldova as its Communist Party leader between 1989 and 1990 and a member of the last Soviet policy-making Communist Party Politburo.

None of the above three is expected to garner more than half the votes in the first round -- required for an outright win. Political analysts say a run-off is on the cards for December 1 between the top two contenders.

Another six candidates considered by most experts as also-rans include the leader of Moldova's Communist Party Vladimir Voronin, the head of the nationalist Party of Democratic Forces Valeriu Matei and four independents.
